extracted.intended_audience: writers, editors, and publishers preparing or proofreading texts that include non-English languages or transliterations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for spelling, transliteration, capitalization, diacritics, word division, and typesetting of languages other than English for publication. Covers both general transliteration principles and language-specific orthographic and typographic practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of compound words
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound words are often but not always divided between their component parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide hyphenation examples (e.g., des-igual, mal-es-tar, semi-es-fe-ra, sub-lu-nar); note exceptions recognized by speakers (e.g., no-so-tros may no longer be treated as a compound). Follow language-specific word-division rules when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Spanish special characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Spanish employs a set of special characters that should be used in Spanish text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult table 11.1 for the specific characters (accented vowels, ñ, ü, etc.). Preserve diacritics appropriate to Spanish orthography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical orthography consideration (Albanian, Turkish, Romanian, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: When working with older texts, determine whether a spelling is conditioned by the time it was used or whether current norms should be followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For languages with orthographic reforms (e.g., Albanian since 1972; Romanian orthographic reforms), editors should take historical context into account and consult authors before altering spellings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish digraphs and special letters in successor languages (Croatian, Bosnian, Serbian, Montenegrin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Successor languages of Serbo-Croatian distinguish certain digraphs and letters consistently in standard orthography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid informal substitutions (e.g., replacing a single special letter with 'dj') and follow the standard alphabet for each modern language; see cross-references for Serbian and Montenegrin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Czech diacritical marks and alternate glyphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Czech uses many diacritical marks; some single glyphs (e.g., d and t with caron) may be rendered with an apostrophe in informal contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct diacritical characters as shown in table 11.1; prefer the actual caron glyph rather than apostrophe when accurate representation is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of polite second-person pronouns (Danish, Norwegian)
rubrics_metrics.description: Polite second-person pronouns (De, Dem, Deres) and the familiar I have historically been capitalized in Danish and Norwegian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that these usages are increasingly rare; do not confuse them with third-person pronouns. Follow contemporary practice for the work being edited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dutch capitalization rules for names and diphthong IJ
rubrics_metrics.description: For Dutch, capitalization of particles with personal names follows specific rules; when a word beginning with the diphthong ij is capitalized, both letters are capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also: when a single letter begins a sentence it is lowercased, but the next word is capitalized; consult section 8.10 for particles with personal names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finnish alphabet includes Swedish characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Swedish is an official language in Finland, Finnish orthography and standard keyboards include the Swedish å.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the Swedish a with ring above where required; consult table 11.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hawaiian ʻokina representation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hawaiian ʻokina (glottal stop) is represented by a left single quotation mark (U+2018) or optionally by a modifier letter turned comma (U+02BB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some publishers/authors prefer U+02BB to differentiate the ʻokina from common punctuation; however, appearance may be identical in many typefaces—discuss preferences with author/publisher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of accented vowels in Hungarian
rubrics_metrics.description: Hungarian uses a wide variety of accented vowels that must be represented accurately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult table 11.1 for specific accented forms required in Hungarian text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Icelandic special letters and capitalization of eth
rubrics_metrics.description: Icelandic includes consonants eth (ð) and thorn (þ) and acute-accented vowels; the eth is never word-initial and is capitalized only in contexts where all capitals are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure correct representation of these letters and their capitalization behavior; see table references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish formal-address capitalization and line-division
rubrics_metrics.description: In formal address, the second-person plural pronoun Państwo (and related forms) is capitalized; Polish word division usually follows syllabic structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: kom-pli-ka-cja; sta-ro-pol-ski. The conjunction 'i' (and) should never be left at the end of a line—carry it to the next line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portuguese capitalization and accented capitals
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles and nouns/adjectives denoting nationality are capitalized as in Spanish; accented capitals, sometimes dropped in running Portuguese text, should always be used when presenting Portuguese in an English context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve accented capitals for clarity in English publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romanian/Moldovan s-cedilla vs s-comma and orthographic reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Romanian and Moldovan use S/Ș and T/Ț (comma below) though cedilla variants often appear; orthographic reforms have changed usage of some letters (e.g., ă vs â or variants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the comma-below forms (the correct modern forms); investigate historical spelling variants and consult author to determine preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serbian and Montenegrin alphabet usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Montenegrin recognizes both Latin and Cyrillic as official; Serbian's standard is Cyrillic (though Latin is also used under law); Montenegrin requires two extra Latin letters (Ś, Ź).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow legal/standard practices for each language and include necessary extra letters for Montenegrin; avoid informal substitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Swedish second-person pronoun capitalization change
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditionally capitalized second-person pronouns Ni and Er are now lowercased in all contexts in Swedish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow contemporary Swedish practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turkish and Azeri orthographic reforms and dotted I
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern Turkish and Azeri alphabets have undergone reforms; the letter i retains its dot when capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Azeri alphabet (since 1992) differs in presence/absence of certain letters (e.g., includes Qq and Xx and letters lacking in Turkish); check period-specific spellings and consult current standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turkmen/Uzbek Latin transitions and special characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Turkmen has transitioned from Cyrillic to Latin; Uzbekistan is transitioning; Uzbek requires the left single quotation mark in letters O‘ and G‘.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for transitional orthographies and include the proper quotation mark where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use transliteration (romanization) in nonspecialized works
rubrics_metrics.description: In nonspecialized works, convert words or phrases from non-Latin alphabets to the Latin alphabet (transliterate/romanize).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use authoritative resources such as ALA-LC Romanization Tables or The World’s Writing Systems; do not attempt transliteration from an unfamiliar language; apply related capitalization, punctuation, and division recommendations from this chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer Unicode fonts for non-Latin alphabets
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors who include non-Latin alphabets should generally opt for fonts that include correct Unicode characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult publisher about font availability; avoid non-Unicode specialized fonts when possible; see also section 2.16 for technical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in proofreading non-Latin alphabets
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone unfamiliar with a non-Latin language should exercise extreme caution when proofreading even single words in that alphabet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grave errors can occur when similar characters are mistaken for each other; query the author if in doubt and consult Unicode numbers and descriptions when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize diacritics in nonspecialized transliteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Except in specialized works, use as few diacritics as needed to aid pronunciation; simplified forms are easier for general readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, prefer Shiva over Śiva for general-audience Hindu-mythology works; Merriam-Webster transliterations are usually preferred in nonspecialized works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italics versus roman for transliterated terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Transliterated terms (other than proper names) that have not become part of English are italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a term is used throughout a work, italicize on first appearance then set in roman thereafter; words listed in dictionaries are usually set in roman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and stick to a transliteration system (Arabic, Hebrew, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is often no universal transliteration system (Arabic, Hebrew, etc.); select one system and use it consistently with as few exceptions as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ALA-LC Romanization Tables, International Journal of Middle East Studies system; consult table 11.2 for preferred Unicode characters for specific marks like hamza and ‘ayn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arabic hamza and ‘ayn representation
rubrics_metrics.description: The hamza (’) and the ‘ayn (‘) frequently appear in transliterated Arabic and must be made clear on every occurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use preferred Unicode modifier letters for hamza and ‘ayn; note some systems drop the hamza at the beginning of a word; in nonspecialized works apostrophe or opening single quote are sometimes used but must be handled with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use familiar English forms for isolated Arabic references
rubrics_metrics.description: Isolated references in text to well-known Arabic persons or places should employ forms familiar to English-speaking readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Avicenna (not Ibn Sina), Damascus (not Dimashq), Mecca (not Makka/Makkah).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arabic definite article hyphenation and assimilation
rubrics_metrics.description: Chicago recommends joining the Arabic definite article al- to a noun with a hyphen (e.g., al-Islam, al-Nafud), though practices vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representation of assimilation is important (e.g., poetry), show assimilations (an-Nafud) but in most situations write article+noun without indicating elision; authors may drop the initial 'a' in certain constructions—confirm conventions with author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of transliterated Arabic
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Arabic has no uppercase/lowercase distinction, practice in transliterated Arabic varies; Chicago recommends capitalizing only the first word and any proper nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat al like 'the': capitalize only at beginning of sentence or title; follow section 11.6 and cross-reference 8.14 and 16.75 for citation and alphabetizing of Arabic personal names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid breaking transliterated Arabic across lines when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Breaking transliterated Arabic words or names at the ends of lines should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If necessary, allow a break after al or Ibn or after two letters if the second has an underdot; never break digraphs dh, gh, kh, sh, th unless both letters have underdots; do not break before/after a hamza; follow English word-division rules otherwise; remember untransliterated Arabic reads right to left—maintain order within lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer Hanyu Pinyin for Chinese romanization
rubrics_metrics.description: Hanyu Pinyin has largely supplanted older systems and is the recommended standard for romanizing Chinese in modern writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Pinyin for writing about China; Library of Congress romanization adopted Pinyin; where older spellings are familiar (Sun Yat-sen, Chiang Kai-shek), exceptions are acceptable; if in doubt consult Merriam-Webster or the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle exceptions and older spellings in Chinese
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain place-names and personal names familiar in older forms may be retained or added parenthetically after the Pinyin form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If changing spellings, consult author; use dictionary authority for names not listed in older forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostrophes, hyphens, and tone marks in Pinyin
rubrics_metrics.description: Pinyin usually omits tone marks in general publications; apostrophes may separate syllables in names (e.g., Xi'an) and are sometimes used to avoid ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Library of Congress Pinyin does not include tone marks; tone marks may be appropriate in language-learning contexts; use apostrophes sparingly to distinguish syllable boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use modified Hepburn for Japanese romanization
rubrics_metrics.description: The modified Hepburn (hyojun) system is the romanization most commonly used outside Japan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use apostrophe after a syllabic n before a vowel or y (Gen', San'yo); use macrons over long vowels (typically ō, ū) except for well-known place names and loanwords that have entered English (Tokyo, shogun), though macrons may be used where pronunciation matters; use hyphens sparingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization and italics for Chinese and Japanese romanized text
rubrics_metrics.description: Romanized personal names and place-names are capitalized; common nouns in English sentences are lowercased and italicized when not assimilated into English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Names of institutions, schools of thought, religions, etc., are capitalized if set in roman, lowercased if in italics. Titles: first word of a romanized title is always capitalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include original Chinese/Japanese characters when helpful
rubrics_metrics.description: Chinese and Japanese characters may be included immediately following the romanized term to aid identification, especially in bibliographies and glossaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where used in running text, enclose characters in parentheses; alert publisher to special-character needs and font requirements; use Unicode-enabled fonts where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hebrew transliteration: choose a system and be consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: Several acceptable romanization systems exist for Hebrew; any may be used provided usage is consistent within the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ALA-LC Romanization Tables are one option; consult table references and Merriam-Webster entries for Hebrew alphabet illustrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hebrew diacritics and specialist marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Transliterated Hebrew sometimes requires underdots, macrons, acute accents, carons, superscript schwa, and other marks in specialist materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are usually reserved for scholarly works; in general-audience works minimize diacritics but maintain internal consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hebrew prefixes and punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hebrew prepositions, conjunctions, and articles often appear as prefixes in romanization; some authors insert apostrophes or hyphens after these prefixes while others do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either approach is acceptable if used consistently throughout a work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hebrew capitalization/italics and internal consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Hebrew has no case distinction, there is no universally used system for capitalizing romanized Hebrew; follow normal English usage for capitalization and italics or eschew capitalization if that is the chosen system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author must ensure internal consistency; follow English usage as needed for names, titles, and emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hebrew and other right-to-left script handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Unromanized Hebrew phrases are read right to left and must retain that order even when embedded in English sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a line break occurs within an unromanized phrase, words must still be read right to left on each line; as a safeguard, authors should highlight Hebrew words and provide instructions on line breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Russian transliteration: choose system suited to audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Many transliteration systems exist for Russian; linguistic journals prefer systems with diacritics, while general-audience works should avoid diacritics and follow the U.S. Board on Geographic Names system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Merriam-Webster spellings for familiar names (e.g., Chekhov, Moscow) where applicable; consult table 11.3 for mappings and Unicode numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve Cyrillic capitalization conventions in transliteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalization conventions in Cyrillic resemble French and should be preserved in transliteration (e.g., pronouns, days, months lowercased; geographic designations capitalized when formal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tverskaya guberniya; moskovskiy universitet; russkiy kompozitor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Russian punctuation conventions (guillemets, dashes, ellipses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Russian uses guillemets (« ») for dialogue and quoted material and dashes for dialogue; ellipses follow French usage and sometimes substitute with question/exclamation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When transliterating or translating Russian dialogue, mimic Russian punctuation conventions as appropriate; in English publications regularize ellipses to three dots if desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Russian word-division rules for transliteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Transliterated Russian should be divided according to the rules governing division in the Cyrillic original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combinations representing single Cyrillic letters (ch, kh, sh, shch, ts, ya, ye, yé, yu, zh) should never be divided; certain consonant clusters are normally not divided but may be if they fall across prefix/root boundaries; prefixes usually should not be divided within themselves; division after vowel/diphthong before a single Cyrillic consonant is allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: South Asian transliteration: diacritics and simplified practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Transliteration of South Asian languages may require many special characters, but many writers use simplified forms that omit diacritics and other markings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 11.2 lists characters; for general audiences simplified styles (e.g., sh for ś) are common, but scholarly works may require full diacritics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek transliteration conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Isolated Greek words/phrases in nonclassic-specialist works are usually transliterated; Greek accents are omitted in transliteration and macrons may be used to distinguish long vowels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transliterate iota subscript as an on the line (e.g., anthropoi), transliterate rough breathing as h, ignore smooth breathing, retain diaeresis in transliteration, italicize transliterated Greek unless words occur frequently (then italicize first mention only).

rubrics_metrics.name: Typesetting Greek and font requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors presenting Greek should use Unicode-enabled fonts if possible; publishers must ensure Greek fonts are available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greek normally not set in italics; adjust type size or add white space when multiple diacritics appear; check Unicode numbers and font support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek breathing marks placement and representation
rubrics_metrics.description: When Greek is set in Greek alphabet, every initial vowel/diphthong/rho must be marked with either a rough or smooth breathing placed over the lowercase vowel or to the left of capital letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single quotation mark is inadequate for a breathing mark because of incorrect size/placement; use proper breathing glyphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek accent marks usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek has three accent marks (acute, circumflex, etc.) that govern pronunciation and should be used appropriately when Greek is set in the original alphabet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When transliterating, accents are omitted; when setting Greek in original characters, ensure correct accent usage and positioning.
